summary: A function pointer stores the address of code instead of data. It lets you choose which function runs at run time, enabling callbacks, jump tables, and plug-in style designs in plain C.

sections.heading: Declaration and call
sections.body: Parentheses around `*name` are mandatory; without them you declare a function returning a pointer. The pointer's return and parameter types must match the target function.
sections.code:
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

int (*fp)(int, int);   // pointer to function(int,int) -> int
fp = add;              // or &add
printf("%d\n", fp(10, 5));   // 15

sections.heading: Properties
bullets: Can be stored in variables, arrays, structs, and passed or returned.

sections.heading: Callbacks
sections.body: Passing a function pointer lets a generic routine call back into your code. The standard `qsort` and `bsearch` work this way.

sections.heading: Arrays of function pointers
sections.body: A table of functions gives a fast dispatch without a long if/else chain.
sections.code:
int (*ops[])(int, int) = { add, sub, mul, div_ };
int r = ops[1](10, 5);   // calls sub

sections.heading: Structs with function pointers
sections.body: Putting function pointers in a struct emulates methods and is how the Linux kernel builds interfaces such as `file_operations`.
Function-pointer syntax is hard to read. Give the type a name once and reuse it.
`qsort` sorts any array by calling your comparator with pointers to two elements. Return negative, zero, or positive. Avoid `a - b` for ints because it can overflow.
Interrupt vectors, VM opcodes, and protocol handlers are often arrays of function pointers indexed by an event or opcode, replacing a switch with a single indirect call.

subtopics.title: Security note
subtopics.summary: Overwritten function pointers are an attack target.

sections.body: If a buffer overflow overwrites a function pointer, the attacker controls where the next indirect call goes. Mitigations include bounds checking, read-only relocations, and control-flow integrity.

takeaways: Use for callbacks, dispatch tables, and struct-based interfaces.
typedef the pointer type for readability.
Check function pointers for NULL before calling.
